Feeding a security monitor

Tell a security monitor what your agents did - a metadata feed of events over a Unix socket and a commit-matching snapshot file, each a small versioned contract, both off by default.

On this page
  • The metadata feed, version 1
  • What a frame carries
  • Class, severity and outcome
  • The two requests
  • Receipts
  • How delivery behaves
  • The commit-matching snapshot, version 1
  • Which repository a session is in
  • Turn on the metadata feed
  • Turn on commit records and the snapshot
  • Recording commits
  • What it does not cover

A security monitor can see processes, files and connections. What it cannot see is what your agents did inside Seamless. Seamless can tell it, in two independent ways:

  1. A metadata feed of events. Every event in Seamless's log - a memory written, a write held, a read refused, a session started - goes to a Unix socket the monitor listens on, as metadata: who, what, where, when and how it went, and never the content.
  2. A commit-matching snapshot. One JSON file, replaced whole every few minutes, lists which sessions ran when and in which repository, which tasks a commit may name, and the commits agents recorded on each. A monitor watching a repository's main branch matches that branch's commits against it: a commit pushed from outside every agent session and every task is the one worth a look.

Both are optional and off by default, and off is exactly the earlier behavior: no socket is dialed, no file is written, and no tool changes shape. Each is a small generic contract, so any program that speaks it can be the monitor. Use either or both.

Metadata feed Commit-matching snapshot
Answers What agents are doing, as it happens Which commits came from tracked work
Delivery HTTP/1.1 batches pushed to a Unix socket One JSON file the monitor reads
Contract Wire format v 1 kind seamless_feed, version 1
Carries Kinds, codes, counts, sizes, flags and ids Session names, task ids, repository names, times and commit ids
Needs Write screening on, and screening.feed_socket commits.snapshot_file; commits.record adds the commit ids

The metadata feed, version 1

With the feed on, the daemon reads its own event log, in the order events landed, from a cursor it keeps in the spool, so a burst never loses an event. Each event becomes one frame, and frames travel in batches to the consumer, the program listening on the socket. The version is the v on every batch header, limits answer and receipt, and it is 1.

Within a version a frame may gain an optional name, one that appears only where it applies, as actor.account did for restricted accounts. A consumer ignores a name it does not know. Removing or renaming a name, or changing what one holds, takes a new version.

What a frame carries

One JSON object per line on the wire, wrapped here to read:

{"time": "2026-11-02T01:16:54.977Z", "host": "build-host",
 "class": "agent", "activity": "memory_held", "severity": "medium", "outcome": "blocked",
 "actor": {"kind": "agent", "id": "4242.1730000000", "session": "cc/0a1b2c3d-4e5f6a7b"},
 "target": {"system": "seamless", "asset": "myapp", "path_class": "memory"},
 "fields": {"event_id": "01KX0000000000000000000020", "hold_id": "01KX0000000000000000000021",
            "item_kind": "memory", "kind": "constraint", "op": "write",
            "reasons": "instruction.override", "source_seq": 4812, "tool": "memory_write"}}
Field What it holds
time When the event happened, UTC to the millisecond
host The daemon's host name, lowercase
class agent, auth, file, config, finding or health
activity The event's kind as one word: memory.held becomes memory_held
severity info, low, medium or high
outcome success, failure, blocked or unknown
actor Who acted: kind agent, with session the session's name and id its agent process (pid and start time); kind user with id owner; or kind system with id seamless. account names a restricted account (below)
target.system seamless
target.asset The project: its slug, global for the global scope, or a keyed hash (below)
target.path_class The item kind, when the event has one
fields The event's metadata

fields comes from an allowlist of metadata keys, each with a pattern its value must fit:

  • Codes and kinds: kind, item_kind, tool, op, hook, via, reason, surface, change, by, action, status, from, to, where, mode, step, outcome, proof.
  • Numbers: size, bytes, memories, notes, projects, added, failures, duration_ms, items, safe, flagged, suppressed, item_count, emitted_tokens.
  • Flags: held, quarantined, baseline, on, updated, truncated, is_error, ambient, favorite, matched.
  • Ids: hold_id, released_hold_id, superseded_by, credential_id, and item_ids joined with commas.
  • Lists of codes, joined with commas: verdicts, reasons.
  • Versions: version, current_version.

Beside those, an event's frame has event_id and, when the event names an item, item_id. access.refused adds target_project, and settings.features_changed adds one feature_<name> flag per feature.

Nothing else reaches a frame, and a value that does not fit its pattern (free text where a code belongs) is dropped. So a frame never carries arguments, results, bodies, prompts, queries, names or titles.

A restricted account names itself. Every event recorded for a restricted local account's request carries actor.account, the account's name, whatever the surface (its agents' tool calls, hooks and A2A recalls) and whatever the event: writes, held proposals, task changes, session starts and ends, and refused reaches, its refusal at the console's door included. In one of its sessions session is the session's qualified name (_example_agent:cc/..., the name the console and seam show); with no session bound the actor is kind agent with account alone. An event filed under one of its sessions names the account even when you caused it, as when you release or discard one of its proposals (those frames carry by owner or released_hold_id in fields):

{"time": "2026-11-12T09:00:00.000Z", "host": "build-host",
 "class": "auth", "activity": "access_refused", "severity": "medium", "outcome": "blocked",
 "actor": {"kind": "agent", "session": "_example_agent:cc/0a1b2c3d-4e5f6a7b", "account": "_example_agent"},
 "target": {"system": "seamless", "asset": "myapp"},
 "fields": {"event_id": "01KX0000000000000000000R01", "reason": "peer.unreachable", "source_seq": 4813,
            "surface": "mcp", "target_project": "h:401a93d78f42331c657f8eea", "tool": "memory_read"}}

Your own events never carry account, so your frames are exactly as they were. An account's name is 1 to 64 of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -, not starting with . or -. A name outside that pattern travels as h: and the first 24 hex digits of the name's SHA-256, so the event still names the account. The hash is not keyed, so the monitor can compute it from its own configuration, and the snapshot below names such an account the same way. A session's name is 1 to 128 of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : / - starting with a letter or digit, or, for a restricted account's session, <account>: followed by such a name, 128 characters in all. A session name outside both is left out; the frame still names the account.

A fenced project travels as a keyed hash. A confidential or sealed project, or one locked under peer_auth, appears only as h: and 24 hex characters, in target.asset and in target_project alike. The key is random and lives in the spool folder as hash.key, so a project's hash is stable across restarts and a monitor can follow one project without learning its name. Remove the key and every project's hash changes.

Class, severity and outcome

Most events are class agent, severity info, outcome success. These are not:

Event Class Severity Outcome
corpus.drift file high; medium for a missing file blocked; unknown for a missing file
lockdown.changed config high going on, medium going off success
access.refused auth medium blocked
memory.held agent medium blocked
settings.features_changed, project.isolation.changed config medium success
update.failed config medium failure
backup.restored file high success
backup.failed, backup.restore_failed file medium failure
backup.deleted file low success
backup.created file info success
memory.screened agent low with a verdict, else info blocked when held, else success
memory.released, memory.discarded, corpus.confirmed, session.tainted, session.untainted agent low success
hook.error agent low failure
update.started, update.applied config low success
update.available config info success
corpus.reviewed finding info success
tool.call agent info failure on a tool error, else success

Write screening's own events, and what each one's payload holds, are in its event table.

A backup event's item is the backup's file name, which is not an id, so no frame names the file. What the frames carry:

Event Fields
backup.created kind (scheduled, manual, before-restore), where (folder or local), bytes, memories, notes, projects
backup.failed kind, where, reason (a fixed word: no-space, export, read-back, database, cancelled, unsafe-file, internal, or folder- and the folder's state), and failures, the automatic streak, for a scheduled backup
backup.deleted kind, where, by (owner, or prune for an old automatic backup)
backup.restored mode (replace or merge), kind, memories, notes, added for a merge that added something, by (console or cli), proof (owner, passkey or account), and credential_id, the id of the approver passkey that approved it
backup.restore_failed mode, reason (a fixed word), and outcome (failed, expired, partial) with step apply, or step stage when the restore could not be prepared

The two requests

Both are HTTP/1.1 on the socket, one request to a connection, and the feed waits up to 30 seconds for an answer.

GET /v1/limits reads the consumer's limits, when the feed starts and hourly after:

{"v": 1, "frame_bytes": 16384, "batch_frames": 500, "batch_bytes": 1048576, "heartbeat_s": 300}

Those values are also the defaults, used until a consumer says otherwise. A value that is missing, zero or negative keeps its default, and an answer that is not status 200 or not version 1 changes nothing. Only heartbeat_s changes what the feed does today. The other three are read but do not narrow what is sent: a batch never exceeds 500 frames or 1 MiB, and a frame never exceeds 16,384 bytes, so a consumer must accept at least the defaults.

POST /v1/batch, with Content-Type: application/x-ndjson, sends a header line and one frame per line, each ending in a newline:

{"v":1,"batch":"<id>","frames":<n>,"dropped":<n>}
{ one frame }
{ one frame }

batch is 1 to 64 of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : -, starting with a letter or digit, and never repeats. frames is how many lines follow. dropped is how many frames the feed has lost that the consumer has not yet recorded.

Receipts

The consumer answers each batch with a JSON receipt, and its action decides:

action HTTP status What the feed does
settle 200 Deletes the batch, and subtracts the receipt's dropped from its count of lost frames
retry The rule's Keeps the batch and sends it again after backing off
discard The rule's Deletes the batch and counts its frames as dropped

A settle carries the batch id, a status of stored or duplicate, the whole numbers frames, accepted, refused_count and dropped, and a refused list:

{"v": 1, "action": "settle", "status": "stored", "batch": "<id>",
 "frames": 2, "accepted": 2, "refused_count": 0, "refused": [], "dropped": 0}

A retry or a discard names one rule, at that rule's status, and a retry may add retry_after_s:

rule Status action
sender 403 retry
path 404 retry
method 405 retry
type 415 retry
version 400 retry
store 503 retry
size 413 discard
newline 400 discard
header 400 discard
frames 400 discard

Any other reply - no JSON, another version, another batch's id, a number missing, a status that does not fit the action - counts as a retry: only a receipt settles or discards a batch. A retry, or a consumer it cannot reach, backs the feed off from 5 seconds, doubling to 5 minutes; a retry_after_s sets the wait inside those bounds.

How delivery behaves

  • One batch in flight, oldest first, resent unchanged, byte for byte, under its id until a receipt settles or discards it, across restarts too.
  • A bounded spool. While the consumer is down the feed spools to feed_spool: at most 10,000 frames and 8 MiB, the oldest dropped first and counted in the next header's dropped.
  • Heartbeats. When nothing else is waiting the feed sends a heartbeat frame every third of the consumer's heartbeat_s, and never more often than every 10 seconds: class health, activity heartbeat, with interval_s, spooled and dropped_count in fields.
  • A running count. fields.source_seq numbers the frames the spool took, so a frame dropped from it shows as a gap.

The commit-matching snapshot, version 1

One JSON object, whose kind and version name the contract. (seamless_feed is the contract's name; this file is not the metadata feed.)

{
  "kind": "seamless_feed",
  "version": 1,
  "host": "build-host",
  "taken_at": "2026-11-02T01:16:54.977Z",
  "since": "2026-10-03T01:16:54.977Z",
  "sessions": [
    {"id": "cc/0a1b2c3d-4e5f6a7b", "repo": "myapp", "started_at": "2026-11-01T09:00:00.000Z",
     "ended_at": "2026-11-01T10:30:00.000Z",
     "commits": ["1111111111111111111111111111111111111111"]},
    {"id": "cx/0f0f0f0f-1e1e1e1e", "repo": null, "started_at": "2026-11-02T01:00:00.000Z",
     "ended_at": null},
    {"id": "_example_agent:cc/5a6b7c8d-9e0f1a2b", "account": "_example_agent", "repo": "myapp",
     "started_at": "2026-11-01T11:00:00.000Z", "ended_at": "2026-11-01T11:40:00.000Z",
     "commits": ["3333333333333333333333333333333333333333"]}
  ],
  "tasks": [
    {"id": "01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV", "repo": "myapp",
     "commits": ["2222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222"]},
    {"id": "01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAW", "account": "_example_agent", "repo": "myapp",
     "commits": ["4444444444444444444444444444444444444444"]}
  ]
}
Field What it holds
host The daemon's host name, lowercase
taken_at When it was built, UTC to the millisecond
since The start of what it covers: snapshot_window before taken_at, or the start of the first session when that is later. A commit seen before it is outside the snapshot
sessions[].id The session's name - the cc/... or cx/... on a briefing's Seam session line, or a sess/* name, and for a restricted account's session its qualified name (_example_agent:cc/...) - so a commit message that mentions it matches. A name outside the contract's pattern, or one another listed session already took, is replaced by the session's ULID
sessions[].account The restricted account that started the session; left out for yours
sessions[].repo The repository the session's working directory is in, or null
sessions[].started_at, ended_at When it started, and when it ended - null while it is active. A session idle longer than gardener.session_idle_minutes has ended at its last activity, the end the idle reaper gives it: never at the moment it was reaped, and whether or not the reaper runs
tasks[].id A task's ULID, for a commit message that names one
tasks[].account The restricted account behind the task: the one whose session recorded one of its commits (the earliest such record), else the one that created it, else the one whose words its text carries. Left out when none is, as for your own tasks
tasks[].repo Its project's repository, when the project maps exactly one; left out otherwise
commits The ids recorded on the session or task, oldest first; left out when there are none

Which entries it lists: every session live at some point since since, and every task that is open or in progress or changed since since (closing a task and recording its commits both change it). Up to 100,000 of each: past that, the sessions that ended earliest are left out and since moves past them, so the snapshot still covers everything it claims to, and the tasks changed least recently are left out.

It carries identifiers and times only: never a finding, a title, a body, a path or a project slug.

Names and patterns. A session id is 1 to 128 of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ : / - starting with a letter or digit, or, for a restricted account's session, an account name and : followed by such a name, 128 characters in all. An account is the name, 1 to 64 of A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ - not starting with . or -, or, for a name outside that, h: and the first 24 hex digits of the name's SHA-256, as the metadata feed sends it.

account within version 1. account, and session ids in the qualified form, appear only for sessions and tasks of a restricted account, so the snapshot of an install that lists none under peer_auth.restricted (the default) is exactly as it was. The check below holds every object to its names, and a consumer that does the same must accept account as optional: one that predates it refuses a snapshot listing a restricted account's work.

The daemon writes the snapshot as it starts and every snapshot_interval after. Each write builds the whole document, checks it against the contract, writes it beside the file and renames it into place, so a reader never sees half of one. The check holds it to exactly the names above (the optional ones - account, commits and a task's repo - may be absent or null), each value of its type and on its pattern, no list past its bound, and no session id, task id or commit in one entry given twice. A snapshot that would break the contract is not written, and the last good file stays.

Which repository a session is in

A session's repository is found from its working directory through the repo map, exactly as its project is (the longest mapped path the directory lies under, on the session's own host). The repository's name is the last segment of its origin remote - git@host:owner/myapp.git gives myapp - or, with no usable origin, the last segment of its path. Configure the monitor with the same names. A working directory outside every mapped repository gives null, and so does a name outside the contract's pattern.

A confidential or sealed project's repository is never named, and neither is that of a project locked under peer_auth. Their sessions and tasks are still listed, with their recorded commits: sessions by name, with their times and a repo of null, and tasks by id, with repo left out. A monitor that matches by time cannot match those sessions; a recorded commit, or one whose message names the session or task, still matches.

Turn on the metadata feed

The feed is part of write screening, so it needs that feature on as well as a socket to deliver to:

features:
  screening: true
screening:
  feed_socket: /path/to/consumer/ingest.sock
  feed_spool: /path/to/spool               # default <data_dir>/feed

SEAMLESS_SCREENING_FEED_SOCKET and SEAMLESS_SCREENING_FEED_SPOOL override the two paths, which expand a leading ~ and must be absolute. They are read at start, so restart the daemon after a change. The feature itself can also be turned on from the console, and takes effect without a restart.

With no socket set the feed never starts. With a socket set and the feature off it sends nothing, and turned on again it starts from the newest event rather than replaying the gap.

The spool folder is the daemon's alone. It is created 0700, and the feed refuses one that is a symbolic link and, on macOS and Linux, one its group or others can reach or another account owns. A feed that cannot start leaves the daemon serving without it, and the log says metadata feed not started.

Turn on commit records and the snapshot

commits:
  record: true                                               # offer the commits argument
  snapshot_file: /path/to/outbox/snapshot-seamless_feed.json # write the snapshot here
  snapshot_interval: 5m                                      # default 5m, from 30s to 24h
  snapshot_window: 720h                                      # default 30 days, from 1h to a year

Each key has an environment override: SEAMLESS_COMMITS_RECORD, SEAMLESS_COMMITS_SNAPSHOT_FILE, SEAMLESS_COMMITS_SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL and SEAMLESS_COMMITS_SNAPSHOT_WINDOW. They are read at start, so restart the daemon after a change. Neither half needs write screening.

record and snapshot_file switch on separately: a snapshot without recorded commits still tells a monitor which sessions ran when, and where. Off, neither tool offers the argument (a call that sends one is refused as an unknown parameter, word for word as before), nothing is recorded, and no file is written.

snapshot_file must be absolute (a leading ~ expands), and its directory must already exist: the daemon creates nothing there but that file (and, for a moment, a hidden temporary file beside it). The file's mode is 0640: put it in a directory only the daemon's account can write and whose group is the monitor's. Whoever can write that directory can replace the snapshot, and with it vouch for any commit.

Recording commits

With record on, both tools list commits in their schema:

  • session_end commits=[...] records the ids on the session being ended - the same session the call completes, behind the same project fence.
  • tasks_update id=<task> commits=[...] records them on the task. Recording is an update like any other: it lands in the same transaction as the rest of the call, and a task another session holds via a live claim refuses it with already claimed, exactly as it refuses a retitle.

The argument takes an array, or a comma-separated string. Each entry must be a full commit id - the 40-character SHA-1 or 64-character SHA-256 name git rev-parse HEAD prints. An abbreviation is refused, never expanded: it can name a different commit once the repository grows a colliding prefix. Uppercase is read as lowercase, and a repeat counts once - within the call, and against what the session or task already holds. One call records at most 256 distinct ids, and one session or task holds at most 10,000. Any bad entry refuses the whole call: a refused session_end leaves the session open, and a refused tasks_update changes nothing, its other fields included.

A successful call reports commits_recorded, and its event (session.ended, task.transition) carries the same count. The ids themselves live in the record, never in an event.

What it does not cover

  • The feed has gaps it can only count. Frames dropped past the spool's bound are counted, not kept. Nothing is spooled while write screening is off. If the event log is rewritten (a restore from an archive, say) and the event the cursor names is gone, the feed resumes at the newest event and logs a warning.
  • A record is an agent's claim. Seamless checks that an id is a full commit id, never that the commit exists or that this session made it. Any caller allowed to end a session or update a task can vouch for a commit on it; the per-call bound keeps an agent from vouching for a whole history in one paste.
  • Agents must pass the ids. Nothing reads git on an agent's behalf. A session that ends through the client's own hook (most Claude Code sessions) records no commits unless the agent called session_end with them; its times and repository still reach the snapshot.
  • A task's recorder needs a session. The snapshot learns who recorded a task's commit from the session the recording call ran in. A commit a restricted account records on a task with no session bound names no recorder, so that task's account falls back to whoever created or rewrote it.
  • The snapshot is the record's view, not git's. Commits that never reached a session's or task's record are matched, if at all, by the monitor's own rules - a message naming a listed session or task, or a commit time inside an open session of the same repository.
